questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the author's primary central argument in the passage?
options: A) GEC-III will fail completely because foreign supply-chain risks for lithium and cobalt make renewable energy infrastructure financially unviable compared to legacy coal generation.
B) Without fundamental reforms in DISCOM pricing structures and legacy contracts, GEC-III’s green infrastructure upgrades cannot overcome the power sector's financial instability.

C) The implementation of GEC-III represents an unconstitutional expansion of central government power that unfairly strips sovereign state regulators of their authority over agricultural tariffs and rural electricity distribution.

D) Although the Green Energy Corridor Phase-III scheme introduces high-voltage transmission lines, co-located battery storage systems, and advanced AI demand-response algorithms to evacuate green power across eight resource-rich states, its overall macroeconomic impact will be limited because state-level DISCOMs prefer long-term thermal contracts over renewable PPAs.
questions.explanation:
Explanation & Analysis:
• Why Option D (Longest Option - 47 words) is INCORRECT: Option D misrepresents the passage. The text explicitly states that DISCOMs are trapped in legacy thermal contracts due to mandatory 'take-or-pay' clauses, not because they 'prefer' thermal contracts. It also focuses on descriptive detail rather than capturing the primary thesis.
• Why Option B is CORRECT: Option B accurately summarizes the primary argument: infrastructure additions (GEC-III) are insufficient unless fundamental DISCOM pricing distortions and legacy contract vices are addressed.
• Option A: Too extreme ('fail completely') and focuses solely on supply chains.
• Option C: Focuses narrowly on federal friction from Paragraph 5 rather than the main theme.

questions.question: Based on Paragraphs 2 and 3, why does the introduction of cheap solar power under GEC-III paradoxically increase the average cost of power supply for DISCOMs?
options: A) Solar power generation drops during evening demand peaks, forcing DISCOMs to buy expensive peak power while remaining contractually bound to pay fixed capacity charges for idling thermal plants.
B) Solar panels degrade faster under high-voltage intra-state transmission corridors, forcing state utilities to spend more on battery replacement than they save on fuel consumption.
C) The Central Financial Assistance subsidy of 35% covers only intra-state lines, leaving DISCOMs fully responsible for paying the remaining 65% out of municipal tax revenues.

D) Because solar power generated during peak off-peak hours must be transmitted across long distance high-voltage lines that require constant algorithmic grid balancing by third-party software engineers, the operational maintenance fees charged by private transmission operators outweigh the cost savings achieved through lower generation costs.
questions.explanation:
Explanation & Analysis:
• Why Option D (Longest Option - 44 words) is INCORRECT: Option D introduces completely fabricated information not supported by the passage ('operational maintenance fees charged by private transmission operators outweigh savings...').
• Why Option A is CORRECT: Directly supported by the text. Midday solar leads to zero/negative spot prices, while evening demand forces DISCOMs to buy expensive peak power while simultaneously paying fixed capacity charges for idling coal plants under 'take-or-pay' clauses.
• Option B: Solar panel degradation is never mentioned in the passage.
• Option C: Misinterprets the 35% grant; the passage notes transmission costs are only <12% of total purchase costs.

questions.question: It can be inferred from the author's discussion of the 'take-or-pay' clauses in Paragraph 3 that:
options: A) Thermal power plant operators will voluntarily cancel legacy PPAs once central battery storage facilities come online.
B) Capital subsidies on transmission infrastructure fail to address the bulk of a DISCOM’s fixed financial liabilities.
C) DISCOMs can eliminate financial losses simply by refusing to purchase power from idling thermal stations.

D) Modernizing intra-state transmission lines through GEC-III grants will automatically reduce the fixed capacity charges that state distribution companies are required to pay under older thirty-year thermal power purchase agreements.
questions.explanation:
Explanation & Analysis:
• Why Option D (Longest Option - 31 words) is INCORRECT: Option D explicitly contradicts the passage. The text states that fixed capacity charges remain fixed regardless of central grants or transmission subsidies.
• Why Option B is CORRECT: Paragraph 3 notes that transmission wheeling accounts for less than 12% of power purchase costs. Thus, subsidizing transmission ignores the main financial burden: fixed capacity charges under legacy thermal PPAs.
• Option A: Thermal operators will enforce contracts, not voluntarily cancel them.
• Option C: Under 'take-or-pay' clauses, DISCOMs must pay fixed charges even if they do not take electricity.

questions.question: The author mentions the 'critical-mineral supply-chain vulnerability' in Paragraph 4 primarily to highlight that:
options: A) India should abandon battery storage technologies in favor of domestic coal-fired thermal expansion.
B) Decarbonizing the energy grid through battery storage replaces foreign fossil fuel dependency with critical mineral import dependency.
C) Advanced Chemistry Cell PLI schemes have successfully eliminated India's reliance on foreign battery manufacturers.

D) Relying on Lithium Iron Phosphate and sodium-ion batteries for grid-scale energy storage is technically inferior to traditional mechanical flywheel storage systems because critical minerals cannot withstand the high desert temperatures encountered across solar parks in Rajasthan and Gujarat.
questions.explanation:
Explanation & Analysis:
• Why Option D (Longest Option - 44 words) is INCORRECT: Option D invents external concepts ('mechanical flywheel storage', 'desert temperatures') nowhere mentioned in the passage.
• Why Option B is CORRECT: Directly captures the author's conclusion in Paragraph 4: policy architects risk swapping 'a fossil-fuel import reliance for a critical-mineral supply-chain vulnerability.'
• Option A: The author calls for institutional reform, not returning to coal.
• Option C: Contradicts the text, which explicitly states India remains heavily dependent on imports despite PLI schemes.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's skepticism regarding the success of GEC-III?
options: A) The central government passes binding legislation allowing DISCOMs to legally terminate legacy thermal PPAs without financial penalty upon adopting green energy tariffs.
B) Artificial intelligence models improve solar generation forecasting accuracy by 15% across Northern India.
C) High-voltage intra-state transmission lines reduce line-loss energy dissipation by 4% during summer months.

D) Global supply prices for lithium carbonate stabilize following the discovery of new domestic mineral reserves in South America, thereby enabling private battery developers to construct grid-scale BESS facilities at a lower initial capital expenditure per megawatt-hour.
questions.explanation:
Explanation & Analysis:
• Why Option D (Longest Option - 41 words) is INCORRECT: Option D addresses battery costs, but the author's core skepticism stems from the financial vice of legacy thermal PPAs and DISCOM pricing distortions. Cheaper battery Capex does not solve the PPA problem.
• Why Option A is CORRECT: The author's primary argument is that DISCOMs are trapped by legacy 'take-or-pay' thermal PPAs. If binding legislation allows DISCOMs to terminate these contracts without penalty, the primary structural barrier identified by the author is removed, severely weakening their skepticism.
• Option B: Paragraph 6 explicitly notes algorithms cannot fix financial or contractual issues.
• Option C: Transmission losses represent a minor component (<12%) of the overall problem.

questions.question: What is the tone and attitude of the author towards 'technocratic enthusiasts' described in the final paragraph?
options: A) Fully endorsement of their automated AI vision for solving grid instability.
B) Mildly critical of their reliance on engineering and algorithmic solutions while ignoring institutional political-economy issues.
C) Dismissive of their technical capability to route electrons accurately across high-voltage transmission lines.

D) Highly appreciative of their efforts to integrate artificial intelligence and predictive algorithms into the national grid while recognizing that minor legal adjustments will be required to ensure total state compliance.
questions.explanation:
Explanation & Analysis:
• Why Option D (Longest Option - 38 words) is INCORRECT: Option D falsely claims the author is 'highly appreciative' and believes 'minor legal adjustments' are enough. The author asserts that deep political courage and structural overhauls are required.
• Why Option B is CORRECT: The author acknowledges that algorithms can route electrons, but criticizes the technocratic belief that technology alone can fix political economy issues like utility bankruptcy and legacy PPAs.
• Option A: Contradicts the text ('technological optimism cannot substitute for institutional reform').
• Option C: Too extreme; the author explicitly grants that algorithms can optimize electron routing.

title: The Epistemic Architecture of Algorithmic Governance in Global Supply Chains
passage:
In the contemporary architecture of transnational commerce, global supply chains have evolved from mechanical logistical pipelines into cognitive neural ecosystems. Driven by predictive analytics and autonomous multi-agent systems, modern trade networks optimize inventory flows, forecast disruptions, and reroute maritime freight in real-time without human intervention. Yet, this digital transformation has generated a profound structural paradox: as logistical efficiency scales exponentially, the epistemic transparency of the underlying economic decisions diminishes inversely. When a decentralized procurement algorithm unilaterally cancels a raw material contract across three continents based on non-linear volatility matrices, the corporate executives nominally in charge are reduced to passive observers of proprietary automated outputs.

This delegation of economic agency to opaque computational models challenges foundational principles of corporate governance and liability. Traditional legal frameworks assume human intentionality—a culpable mind or negligent oversight—as the prerequisite for assigning commercial liability. When a proprietary optimization subroutine executes a flash liquidation of warehouse assets during an unpredicted localized labor strike, isolating the locus of fault becomes an intricate exercise in forensic software auditing. Is the liability borne by the software engineer who wrote the heuristic code three years prior, the local logistics manager who failed to override the automated warning, or the machine-learning model itself, which synthesized thousands of unstructured historical variables into an uninterpretable decision pathway? Because existing corporate tort laws do not recognize autonomous software as legal agents, firms increasingly resort to algorithmic obfuscation to shield themselves from regulatory penalties.

The friction between algorithmic autonomy and institutional accountability is further intensified by the phenomenon of data monocultures. Modern supply chain networks rely heavily on standardized cloud infrastructure and centralized machine learning models provided by a handful of oligopolistic technology conglomerates. When thousands of independent manufacturing enterprises calibrate their inventory thresholds using identical predictive algorithms, the entire global market begins to exhibit synchronized behavioral patterns. During systemic shocks—such as sudden geopolitical trade embargoes or climate-induced port closures—these synchronized networks fail to self-correct through decentralized market friction. Instead, they execute identical automated withdrawal strategies simultaneously, transforming localized supply bottlenecks into systemic, multi-sector liquidity cascades that defy traditional macroeconomic stabilization tools.

Furthermore, the ideological narrative surrounding digital supply chain optimization often obscures distributional inequities beneath a veneer of mathematical neutrality. Proponents argue that algorithmic markets eliminate human bias, optimize resource allocation, and minimize carbon footprints through rigorous mathematical precision. However, optimization functions are inherently normative value judgments translated into quantitative code. An algorithm optimized strictly for cost minimization and delivery speed will systematically deprioritize labor safety standards in developing manufacturing hubs, subcontracting environmental externalities to vulnerable communities while maximizing short-term shareholder returns. The mathematical abstraction of human labor into passive data vectors sanitizes the human cost of globalized production, wrapping structural exploitation in an impenetrable cloak of computational inevitability.

Critics of hyper-optimized logistical networks advocate for the introduction of mandatory 'algorithmic friction'—deliberate regulatory interventions designed to reintroduce human oversight, operational redundancy, and institutional deliberation into automated trade pathways. They argue that economic resilience is fundamentally incompatible with radical efficiency. Just as biological ecosystems require redundant species diversity to survive viral pathogens, robust commercial networks require structural inefficiencies and human discretion to absorb black swan disruptions without catastrophic collapse. Opponents of this approach, however, contend that imposing bureaucratic friction on digital logistics would cripple competitive advantage in fast-moving global markets, sentencing economies to sluggish output and inflated consumer costs.

Ultimately, the digital reconfiguration of global commerce reveals that technological acceleration outpaces the normative evolution of institutional governance. As autonomous algorithms assume control over the vital circulation of global capital and material goods, society faces an urgent imperative: to redesign the legal and ethical parameters of digital architectures before automated efficiency permanently erodes human autonomy. Until institutional frameworks evolve to pierce the veil of algorithmic opacity, global supply chains will continue to operate not as democratic instruments of shared prosperity, but as opaque, self-referential technocracies governing international trade from behind closed code repositories.

questions.question: Which of the following can be most logically inferred regarding corporate executives and autonomous procurement algorithms based on the passage?
options: A) Executives retain absolute legal control over procurement contracts because they write the baseline rule sets executed by deep learning models.
B) The increasing reliance on autonomous computational models transforms human oversight into a superficial formality, detaching corporate leadership from actual economic decision-making processes.
C) Corporate leaders intentionally deploy opaque algorithms to completely eliminate accountability and bypass international trade laws during labor strikes.

D) Executives successfully utilize traditional corporate governance frameworks to accurately assign tort liability directly to the machine-learning models whenever supply chains experience localized disruptions.
questions.explanation: The correct inference is B, as the passage notes that corporate executives are reduced to 'passive observers of proprietary automated outputs' when algorithms make decentralized decisions. Option D is incorrect because the passage explicitly states assigning fault is an intricate challenge and laws do not recognize AI as agents. Option A contradicts the text stating executives are passive observers. Option C introduces intent ('intentionally deploy... to completely eliminate') not supported by the text.

questions.question: The author discusses 'data monocultures' in paragraph 3 primarily to explain how:
options: A) centralized technology oligopolies eliminate all geopolitical trade embargoes through advanced cloud infrastructure.
B) standardized predictive algorithms create synchronized behavioral vulnerabilities that turn localized bottlenecks into systemic economic cascades.
C) independent manufacturing enterprises successfully self-correct during systemic market shocks without requiring algorithmic oversight.
D) decentralized market friction naturally resolves localized supply chain disruptions before they reach international shipping networks.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because paragraph 3 highlights that standardized algorithms cause synchronized behaviors that transform localized bottlenecks into systemic liquidity cascades. Option A and C directly contradict the text. Option D is incorrect as the text states networks fail to self-correct during shocks.

questions.question: Which of the following best characterizes the author's perspective regarding the claim that algorithmic markets are characterized by 'mathematical neutrality'?
options: A) The author views mathematical neutrality as an objective standard that successfully eliminates human bias from global supply chains.
B) The author considers mathematical neutrality to be a misleading ideological facade that disguises underlying normative value judgments and structural labor exploitation.
C) The author argues that mathematical neutrality is an unachievable technical ideal that will eventually be solved by advanced cloud oligopolies.
D) The author believes that mathematical neutrality directly guarantees safe labor standards and environmental protection in developing manufacturing sectors.
questions.explanation: Option B captures the author's argument in paragraph 4 that optimization functions are normative value judgments wrapped in computational inevitability, masking exploitation. Options A, C, and D misrepresent the passage's critical view.

questions.question: The biological analogy introduced in paragraph 5 ('Just as biological ecosystems require redundant species diversity...') serves to support which of the following assertions?
options: A) Commercial networks require deliberate inefficiencies and human discretion to survive unexpected systemic shocks without failing catastrophically.
B) Radical commercial efficiency is the sole biological mechanism capable of preventing global economic collapse during black swan events.
C) Viral pathogens in international shipping corridors can be eradicated exclusively through automated multi-agent inventory pipelines.
D) Ecosystem degradation in developing nations is caused by a lack of species diversity in cloud computing infrastructure.
questions.explanation: Option A accurately reflects the analogy used to argue that economic resilience requires structural inefficiencies and human discretion (redundancy) just like ecosystems need species diversity. The other options are absurd distortions.

questions.question: Based on the text, what is the primary objection raised by opponents of 'algorithmic friction'?
options: A) Regulatory interventions would eliminate all corporate tax liabilities across developing manufacturing nations.
B) Bureaucratic friction would severely impair competitive advantage, resulting in sluggish economic output and higher consumer costs.
C) Imposing human oversight would completely prevent black swan disruptions and eliminate trade embargoes permanently.
D) Artificial intelligence models would spontaneously achieve legal personhood and demand independent representation.

questions.question: Which of the following conclusions can be drawn regarding the current relationship between technological innovation in supply chains and institutional legal frameworks?

B) Technological innovation has far outpaced institutional governance, leaving commercial networks operating under opaque technocracies devoid of democratic oversight.
C) International trade treaties have completely eliminated algorithmic opacity by forcing tech conglomerates to open their source code repositories.
D) Global supply chains have transitioned away from digital automation and returned entirely to mechanical logistical pipelines.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct, summarizing the recurring theme that technological acceleration outpaces institutional governance and creates opaque technocracies. Options A, C, and D directly contradict the passage's conclusion.

passage:
Between 5 and 12 October the Nobel committees announce this year’s laureates, in a week that has become a ritual of the scientific calendar. The cash award has been raised to 12 million Swedish crowns per prize, from 11 million last year, a sum that is trivial beside the research budgets of the laboratories it honours and yet, by common consent, the least important part of the award. What the money buys is attention. A Nobel turns a specialist into a public figure, a subfield into a headline and, in the cases that matter to a university or a country, a statistic in an informal league table of national scientific achievement. It is worth asking what, precisely, this apparatus measures, since the answer is less obvious than the ceremony suggests.

Begin with arithmetic. The statutes cap any prize at three laureates and, outside peace, reserve it for individuals rather than teams or institutions. These limits were sensible when discoveries were made by a lone experimenter at a bench. They sit awkwardly with a science that now routinely involves collaborations of hundreds or thousands of authors, as in particle physics or genome sequencing. The committee must therefore compress a distributed achievement into three names, and every compression involves a judgement about what counts as the decisive contribution: the idea, the experiment, the instrument, or the leadership that made the work possible. The history of the prizes contains well-known cases of names left off: Lise Meitner, whose part in the discovery of nuclear fission went unrecognised when her collaborator Otto Hahn received the 1944 chemistry prize, and Jocelyn Bell Burnell, whose observation of pulsars preceded the 1974 physics prize awarded to her supervisor and a colleague. Such omissions are usually presented as injustices, and sometimes they are. But the structural point is wider: a rule that fixes the number of winners in advance makes the omission of someone certain whenever the contributors outnumber the places.

The second feature is delay. The prize rewards work whose significance has been established by time, which is why it typically honours discoveries made decades earlier. Peter Higgs proposed his mechanism in 1964 and was recognised in 2013, after experiments had confirmed it; the modification of messenger RNA that underlies the vaccines of the pandemic years was reported in the mid-2000s and honoured in 2023, once it had been tested on a global scale. The delay has a defensible rationale, that a committee should not reward errors, and an awkward consequence: the prize is a lagging indicator. It tells us what a community came to believe about the past, not what is most promising now, and it can serve as a guide to the present only for those who forget that the frontier is, by definition, the part that has not yet been validated.

Third, prizes act on the system they observe. The sociologist Robert Merton described a “Matthew effect” in science, whereby eminent researchers receive disproportionate credit for work done jointly with lesser-known colleagues, and credit begets resources, which beget further credit. A Nobel is the limiting case of the process. Laureates attract students, funding and invitations; their fields attract talent; and those fields appear in retrospect to have been where the important work was done. Part of that appearance is real and part is manufactured, since attention is a cause as well as an effect of progress. Nor are the categories neutral. There are prizes for physics, chemistry and medicine but none for mathematics or geology, and the economics prize, established by Sweden’s central bank in 1968 and not by Alfred Nobel’s will, is not strictly a Nobel at all. The 2024 physics prize for work on artificial neural networks showed the categories stretching to accommodate a field that had grown up largely outside them. Disciplines that fit the existing labels are visible to the public; those that do not tend to be less so.

Defenders reply that these criticisms confuse a prize with a ranking. No one claims the laureates are the only deserving candidates; the prize identifies discoveries of exceptional consequence, and does so with a care few honours match, relying on nominations from invited experts and years of deliberation, with the committee’s records sealed for fifty years. The attention it generates is a public good: it draws students to science and persuades legislatures to fund it. The incentive argument is subtler. If scientists work for recognition as well as for truth, the prospect of a few conspicuous prizes may encourage risk-taking in a system that otherwise rewards the safe and the publishable. The difficulty is that it may equally encourage the opposite: a concentration of effort on fields thought to be prize-worthy, and neglect of the slow, collective and unglamorous work, such as the maintenance of datasets and instruments, on which glamorous discoveries rely.

The record also contains a reminder that the committees’ judgement is not infallible. The 1949 medicine prize to Egas Moniz for the lobotomy is now regarded as one of the prize’s great embarrassments. Its lesson is not that prizes should be abandoned but that the endorsement they carry is the endorsement of a particular moment, given by a small group on the evidence then available. When a prize is read as the final verdict of science, the error lies with the reader and not with the institution.

The most defensible way to read a Nobel announcement, then, is as evidence about the state of consensus in a community, with the biases built into it by its rules: a delay, a numerical limit, a set of categories drawn up in the 1890s and an electorate of invited insiders. Read that way it is informative, though no more authoritative than any other lagging indicator. Read as a measure of the best science done, it conceals as much as it discloses: the collaborators who were not counted, the fields that had no category, and the discoveries that still await the verdict of time. The attention it commands is real. What it should command, in a sensible reader, is not deference but a second question: whom does this prize not name, and why?

questions.question: The author’s mention of Meitner and Bell Burnell is used chiefly to suggest that
options: A) Nobel committees have consistently undervalued the work of women and junior researchers, and this bias is the main flaw of the process
B) the lone experimenter of earlier times has disappeared from modern science, so that no discovery now can be credited to any single person
C) a numerical cap makes someone’s omission certain whenever contributors outnumber the places
D) the omissions were corrected in later years, when the committees acknowledged their mistakes and awarded the missing researchers separate prizes
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option C is Correct: Paragraph 2 says such omissions are ‘usually presented as injustices, and sometimes they are’, but the ‘structural point is wider’: fixing the number of winners guarantees omission when contributors exceed places. The examples illustrate a structural consequence, not a pattern of prejudice.

• Why Option A is Wrong: ‘Consistently’ and ‘main flaw’ attribute a motive the author deliberately sets aside in favour of a structural point; the passage names no pattern by gender or seniority.
• Why Option B is Wrong: Overstated: the author says collaborations are now common, not that no discovery can be credited to one person.
• Why Option D is Wrong: The passage says nothing about later correction or separate prizes; this invents a happy ending.

💡 Approach: When an author cites examples, find the sentence that begins ‘But’; it carries the real point. Here, the structural claim is stated in the final sentence of the paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim that a Nobel Prize is a “lagging indicator”?
options: A) Most recent prizes were awarded within a few years of the cited work.
B) Many laureates were already among the most cited scientists in their fields at the time the prize was announced to them in October.
C) Several prizes have been given for work whose conclusions were later revised in the light of evidence that emerged long afterwards.
D) The committees consult a wide range of invited experts and keep their records sealed for fifty years after each decision has been made.
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option A is Correct: Paragraph 3 rests the claim on a long gap between discovery and award. If most prizes follow the work within a few years, the gap, and so the description of the prize as lagging, is undermined.

• Why Option B is Wrong: High citations before the award show the laureates were already prominent; they do not say how long after the discovery the prize came.
• Why Option C is Wrong: Later revision bears on whether committees err (para 6), not on how long they wait.
• Why Option D is Wrong: Consultation and sealed records concern the process, not the timing.

💡 Approach: Isolate what the claim depends on (the time gap). A weakener attacks that dependence; options about quality of work or process leave it untouched.

questions.question: The statement that attention is “a cause as well as an effect of progress” is best illustrated by which of the following?
options: A) A field wins prizes because its results are demonstrably more important than those of the fields that have never been given a category.
B) A committee honours a discovery only after experiments have confirmed it, so that the prize follows and records an established success.
C) A researcher who is already eminent receives credit for a joint paper that is disproportionate to the part played by junior authors.
D) A field that wins a prize attracts funding and recruits, and so yields results that later seem to justify the prize.
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option D is Correct: Paragraph 4: laureates attract students and funding, their fields attract talent, and those fields appear in retrospect to have been where the work was done. Attention (the prize) feeds back into the progress it seems merely to reward, which is the two-way relation described.

• Why Option A is Wrong: This makes attention purely an effect of prior importance; the causal arrow runs only one way.
• Why Option B is Wrong: Also one-way: the prize follows success (para 3), with no feedback into the progress.
• Why Option C is Wrong: This is the Matthew effect of credit within a project, not attention feeding back into a field’s later progress.

💡 Approach: For ‘best illustrates’ questions, extract the abstract structure (a loop in which effect becomes cause) and reject examples with a one-way arrow.

questions.question: The author’s treatment of the incentive argument implies that
options: A) conspicuous prizes inevitably reduce risk-taking, since scientists will always prefer safe work that is certain to be published
B) the same prospect of prizes could encourage risk-taking and also distort effort towards fashionable fields
C) recognition is a poor motive for scientists, who ought to work only for truth and who are corrupted by the hope of any prize
D) the maintenance of datasets and instruments deserves its own Nobel category, so that collective work can be honoured as individuals are
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option B is Correct: Paragraph 5 calls the argument ‘subtler’: prizes may encourage risk-taking, but ‘equally’ may concentrate effort on prize-worthy fields and neglect unglamorous work. The implication is a double-edged effect.

• Why Option A is Wrong: ‘Inevitably’ and ‘always’ are absolutes; the author grants that prizes may encourage risk-taking.
• Why Option C is Wrong: The author accepts that scientists work for recognition ‘as well as for truth’ and does not moralise about it.
• Why Option D is Wrong: No such proposal is made; the passage only notes the neglect of such work.

💡 Approach: ‘Implies’ questions favour balanced, two-sided options when the author uses words such as ‘subtler’ and ‘equally’.

questions.question: Each of the following is presented as limiting what a Nobel announcement can tell us EXCEPT
options: A) the cap of three names for each prize, which forces a choice about which contribution was the decisive one among many
B) the delay between a discovery and its award, which makes the prize a record of what a community came to believe earlier
C) the fixed set of categories, which leaves some disciplines without a prize and so makes them less visible to the public
D) the sealing of committee records for fifty years, which shields the process from scrutiny
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option D is Correct: Sealed records appear in paragraph 5 as part of the care the defenders cite in the prize’s favour, not as a limitation the author criticises. The other three are limits discussed in paragraphs 2, 3 and 4.

• Why Option A is Wrong: Limitation discussed in paragraph 2 (the rule of three).
• Why Option B is Wrong: Limitation discussed in paragraph 3 (delay, the ‘lagging indicator’).
• Why Option C is Wrong: Limitation discussed in paragraph 4 (categories and visibility).

💡 Approach: In EXCEPT questions, match each option to a paragraph; the odd one out will be used for a different purpose (here, the defenders’ case).

questions.question: The author’s closing question, “whom does this prize not name, and why?”, is best read as
options: A) an accusation that the committees deliberately exclude deserving scientists in order to protect the reputation of the prize and its sponsors
B) a prompt to treat a prize as evidence with built-in biases rather than as a final verdict
C) a call for the abolition of the prizes, since the omissions that the author has described cannot be corrected by any reform of the rules
D) an admission that the author cannot decide whether prizes help or harm science, and so leaves the whole matter to the judgement of readers
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option B is Correct: The last paragraph asks for ‘not deference but a second question’ and reads announcements as evidence about consensus with biases ‘built into it by its rules’. The closing question invites that critical reading.

• Why Option A is Wrong: The author attributes omissions to structure (rules), not to deliberate exclusion or reputation-protection.
• Why Option C is Wrong: Para 6 says the lesson is ‘not that prizes should be abandoned’; this contradicts it.
• Why Option D is Wrong: The author does reach a view (prizes are informative but limited); the question sharpens that view and is not a confession of indecision.

💡 Approach: Tie closing rhetorical questions to the author’s stated thesis. Reject options that radicalise (accusation, abolition) or retreat (indecision).

title: The Border Tax on Carbon: Climate Policy or Trade Policy in Disguise?
passage:
When the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism moved from its reporting-only phase into its definitive phase at the start of 2026, it completed a transformation that critics had long predicted and supporters had long insisted would never happen: a climate measure acquired the machinery of a tariff. Importers of steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen must now surrender certificates corresponding to the emissions embedded in their goods, priced to track what European producers pay under the Union's own emissions trading system. The stated logic is deceptively tidy. If Europe asks its factories to pay for carbon but lets cheaper, dirtier imports enter untaxed, production will simply migrate to jurisdictions with laxer rules, a phenomenon called carbon leakage, and the planet will emit as much as before while Europe deindustrialises. A border adjustment, on this reading, merely levels a playing field that the Union's own ambition had tilted.

The difficulty is that a level field is not the same as a fair one, and the two ideas are routinely conflated in the policy's defence. Exporting countries observe that the mechanism measures carbon intensity at the factory gate but takes no account of the circumstances that produced it. A blast furnace in a developing economy that runs on coal-fired grid power is not dirty because its owners are indifferent to the climate; it is dirty because the grid on which it depends was built, under conditions of scarce capital, to deliver electricity at the lowest immediate cost. To tax the steel is, in effect, to tax the grid, and thereby the stage of development, of the country of origin. The Union's rejoinder is that it is levying a price on emissions, not passing a judgement on virtue, and that any exporter who decarbonises can escape the charge altogether. Each claim is accurate on its own terms. That both remain accurate, and the quarrel remains unsettled, is what makes the dispute durable.

Consider the asymmetry of exposure. Large economies with diversified export markets can absorb a cost imposed by one destination: if Europe becomes less attractive, shipments are redirected elsewhere, and the loss is a matter of margin rather than survival. Smaller exporters, whose covered goods flow overwhelmingly to a single European market, enjoy no such flexibility. Their exposure relative to the size of their economies can exceed that of far bigger producers whose absolute payments are higher. The headline figure, total certificates purchased, thus conceals the more politically explosive one: who bears the cost relative to what they can afford. A mechanism designed with uniform rules produces distinctly unequal consequences, a pattern familiar to anyone who has watched a flat tax meet an uneven distribution of income.

Defenders point to design features that soften the edge. Importers below a modest annual volume are exempt, which spares small traders the paperwork; carbon prices already paid in the exporting country can be deducted; and the free allowances that European industry has enjoyed are being withdrawn gradually as border charges phase in. This last feature is quietly revealing. The two instruments are meant to move in tandem, domestic protection falling as border protection rises, precisely because the Union cannot be seen to shield its producers twice. Yet the phase-out is slow and the design intricate, and intricacy carries its own cost. Compliance requires emissions data verified by accredited auditors. A multinational steelmaker with a dedicated sustainability office can furnish this without strain; a mid-sized exporter in a developing country must first purchase the capacity to prove its emissions before it can begin to reduce them. The administrative burden functions as a fixed cost, and fixed costs favour the large.

A subtler worry concerns what the policy reveals about the architecture of global climate cooperation. The Paris framework rests on the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities: richer nations, having emitted more over time, should carry more of the burden. A unilateral border charge sits uneasily with that principle, because it enforces a single carbon price on the world according to the preferences of one large market. Proponents counter that differentiated responsibility was never meant to be a licence for free-riding, and that, after decades of negotiation yielding pledges without prices, unilateral pricing is the only lever that moves behaviour. The honest observer must concede that both parties are partly right, and that the disagreement is therefore less about facts than about which failure, unequal burdens or inadequate action, one considers the graver.

Meanwhile, the response of exporters has been less ideological than the debate implies. Several large producers are quietly rebuilding their cost structures: signing contracts for renewable power, investing in processes that burn less coal, and lobbying to have domestic carbon markets recognised so that payments made at home can be credited abroad. In this sense the border charge functions less as a wall than as a price signal that arrives earlier than domestic politics would have produced one. Whether that signal accelerates a just transition or merely redirects the dirtiest production towards markets that ask no questions is an empirical matter that will not be settled for years. Trade diversion could leave global emissions unchanged while rearranging who sells to whom, in which case the measure will have achieved the Union's competitive goals without its environmental ones.

The most defensible conclusion is not that the mechanism is wise or foolish but that it is a hybrid whose character will be decided by how it is administered. Applied with generosity, through technical assistance, recognition of foreign carbon prices, and revenue recycled towards the exporters least able to adapt, it could resemble a climate policy that happens to use trade tools. Applied with rigidity, it will resemble a trade policy that happens to use climate language. The text of the regulation is the same in both cases; the difference lies in the discretion exercised afterwards, and discretion is precisely what the affected countries have the least power to influence.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred from the author's distinction between a "level" field and a "fair" one in the second paragraph?
options: A) Because carbon intensity is measured at the factory gate, the mechanism ends up penalising exporters who have been indifferent to climate goals.
B) A uniform carbon price cannot be described as fair unless the revenue it raises is returned in full to the exporting countries.
C) Identical rules can still spread costs unevenly, since carbon intensity partly reflects a country's stage of development.
D) Fairness would require the Union to abandon pricing imported carbon altogether, since any level playing field is inherently unjust.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option C
The author argues that identical treatment (a level field) ignores why a producer is carbon-intensive: coal-heavy grids were built under capital scarcity, so taxing the steel is effectively taxing the stage of development. Uniform rules therefore produce uneven burdens, which is exactly what the option states.

Option A is wrong. The author explicitly says the furnace is not dirty because owners are indifferent to the climate. The option states the exact opposite of the paragraph.
Option B is wrong. The author never links fairness to returning revenue; that idea appears only in the closing paragraph as a possible administrative choice, not as a condition of fairness in paragraph 2. This is an over-extension.
Option D is wrong. Extreme and unsupported. The author questions whether level equals fair, but never argues that the Union should drop the charge or that level fields are unjust.

questions.question: The author regards the dispute between the Union and the exporting countries as "durable" principally because
options: A) each side relies on a valid premise, yet each answers a different question about what the charge is meant to do.
B) the empirical evidence on carbon leakage is too inconclusive to support either the Union's position or the exporters' position.
C) exporting countries have declined to engage with the technical standards the Union has set for reporting and verifying emissions.
D) the Union has been unwilling to defend the mechanism in any terms other than the competitiveness of its own industry.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option A
The author says that each claim is accurate on its own terms yet the quarrel is unsettled. The exporters speak about what the charge does (it taxes development), while the Union speaks about what it intends (a price on emissions, with an exit route). Valid premises answering different questions keep the dispute alive.

Option B is wrong. The author never calls the evidence on leakage inconclusive; she calls both claims accurate. The problem is not lack of evidence.
Option C is wrong. Verification standards are discussed in paragraph 4 as a burden, not as something exporters refuse to engage with. Unsupported by the text.
Option D is wrong. The Union's rejoinder is explicitly framed in climate terms (a price on emissions, escape by decarbonising). The competitiveness rationale appears only in paragraph 1 as the stated logic of the policy.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim in the third paragraph that uniform rules yield "distinctly unequal consequences"?
options: A) Large producers with diversified export markets also report that their margins on sales to the Union have narrowed since the definitive phase began.
B) Covered goods from smaller exporters now make up a growing share of the Union's total imports of steel and aluminium.
C) The price of border certificates has recently risen faster than the price of allowances in the Union's own emissions trading system.
D) Certificate revenue is channelled into transition funds that mostly reach single-market exporters, offsetting their higher relative exposure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option D
The claim concerns unequal consequences, meaning who bears the cost relative to what they can afford. If compensation flows disproportionately to the most exposed exporters, the net consequences become more equal, which directly undercuts the author's claim.

Option A is wrong. Large producers losing margin does not remove the inequality; the claim is about relative burden, and smaller exporters can still be hit far harder. It is a plausible-looking but non-weakening statement.
Option B is wrong. A growing import share says nothing about how costs are distributed relative to capacity. It is irrelevant to the claim, and might even sharpen their dependence.
Option C is wrong. A price movement affects all exporters and does not address whether the burden is unequal across them. Irrelevant.

questions.question: The author calls the simultaneous withdrawal of free allowances and phasing-in of border charges "quietly revealing" because it suggests that the Union
options: A) has persuaded European industry to accept a gradual loss of its free allowances in return for continued access to export markets.
B) is conscious that it must not appear to protect its own producers through two channels at the same time.
C) regards the border charge as a temporary device that will lapse once domestic carbon pricing has become fully effective.
D) expects exporters to pass the entire cost of border certificates on to European consumers through higher import prices.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option B
The paragraph states that the two instruments move in tandem precisely because the Union cannot be seen to shield its producers twice. What is revealed is the Union's sensitivity to how the policy will look, so the correct option captures that awareness.

Option A is wrong. No bargain between industry and the Union is mentioned. This introduces an unsupported trade-off.
Option C is wrong. Nothing suggests the border charge is temporary; it is described as the counterpart of a phase-out, not as something that will lapse.
Option D is wrong. Pass-through to consumers is never discussed. The paragraph is about protection of producers, not about incidence on consumers.

questions.question: The author's treatment of the argument over "common but differentiated responsibilities" in the fifth paragraph is best described as
options: A) sympathetic to the exporters, since a unilateral charge is shown to contradict the framework agreed at Paris.
B) sceptical of both parties, since decades of negotiation have shown that pledges without prices are worthless.
C) even-handed, locating the disagreement in differing priorities rather than in disputed facts.
D) supportive of the Union, since the paragraph concedes that unilateral pricing is the only lever that changes behaviour.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option C
The author states that both parties are partly right and that the dispute is about which failure, unequal burdens or inadequate action, one considers graver. That is a disagreement of priorities, not of facts, and the author does not side with either.

Option A is wrong. The author says the charge sits uneasily with the principle, but then reports the proponents' rebuttal and concludes both are partly right. Calling this sympathetic to exporters overstates it.
Option B is wrong. The author attributes the claim about pledges without prices to proponents; the author does not endorse it, and does not call pledges worthless.
Option D is wrong. The claim that unilateral pricing is the only lever is the proponents' argument, which the author reports but does not adopt.

questions.question: Which of the following best reflects the author's final position on the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism?
options: A) Whether it works as climate policy or as trade policy will depend less on its wording than on the discretion used in applying it.
B) It should be judged primarily by whether it lowers global emissions, since any gains in competitiveness for the Union are of secondary importance.
C) Its defects are largely procedural, and could be corrected by exempting smaller exporters and simplifying the verification process it demands.
D) Its legitimacy ultimately depends on the Union being willing to revise the text of the regulation in response to criticism from exporting countries.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option A
The final paragraph says the mechanism is a hybrid whose character is decided by how it is administered, and that the text is the same in both cases while discretion differs. The correct option restates this.

Option B is wrong. The author raises the emissions test (trade diversion) as an open empirical question but never says it is the primary yardstick, nor that competitiveness is secondary.
Option C is wrong. The author does mention exemptions and administrative burden, but calls the issue broader than procedure; the conclusion is about discretion, not a procedural repair list.
Option D is wrong. The conclusion says the text is the same in both cases and that the difference lies in discretion afterwards. Revising the text is not what the author says matters.

title: The Doorway and the House: India's Social Security Code and the Gig Worker
passage:
When India's labour codes came into force in late 2025, the Code on Social Security did something earlier statutes had avoided: it gave gig and platform workers a name. Delivery riders, ride-hailing drivers and freelance task-performers were defined as distinct categories, and the companies that connect them to customers were designated aggregators, who may be required to contribute a share of their turnover to a fund from which welfare schemes are financed. The recognition is real, and it has been widely welcomed. But recognition is a statement about vocabulary, and the harder question concerns what the vocabulary obliges anyone to do.

The architecture chosen is revealing. Rather than declare these workers employees, entitled to the provident fund and insurance that accompany a payroll, the Code constructs a separate, scheme-based track. Benefits flow from schemes that governments may notify, financed partly by aggregator contributions that are capped at a fraction of what platforms pay out to workers. To receive anything, a worker must register. The design thus treats the gig worker as neither an employee nor an independent contractor in the old sense, but as a third kind of creature for whom protection is available by application rather than by right. Supporters see pragmatism: classifying millions of workers as employees overnight would have been administratively impossible and, platforms argue, commercially ruinous. Critics see a ceiling disguised as a floor.

Underlying the disagreement is an old question in a new form: who is the worker's employer when an algorithm assigns the job, sets the price and can deactivate the account? Platforms maintain that they supply a marketplace, that workers choose when to log in and which orders to accept, and that autonomy is the very feature workers value. Yet autonomy of this kind is partly illusory when the payment for each task is set by software and acceptance rates affect future allocation. A worker who is free to decline orders is not free in the sense that matters if declining carries a penalty that the worker cannot see. The law's silence on this point is conspicuous; the Code asks who contributes, not who controls.

Consider next the matter of portability. Many workers do not serve a single platform; they move between several in a day, following whichever offers the better rate. Contributions that are calculated as a share of each platform's turnover or payouts, and administered through registration, assume that each worker can be attributed to a platform, or at least that earnings can be aggregated across them. If a worker's income is fragmented, the benefit attributable to any one platform's contribution may be too thin to be meaningful, while the data needed to stitch the fragments together raises questions of privacy and verification that the framework has only begun to address. Portability, in other words, is not an optional refinement; it is the condition on which a scheme financed platform by platform can serve workers who do not live platform by platform.

Then there is the matter of incidence. Aggregators will not necessarily absorb new contributions; they may pass them on to customers through higher prices, or to workers through lower payments per task. Which of these occurs depends less on legislative intent than on market structure. Where competition between platforms is intense and customers are sensitive to price, platforms have little room to raise what they charge, and the burden may drift towards the party with the weakest bargaining position: the worker. Where a few firms dominate, they may absorb the cost or pass it on at will. A levy designed to protect workers could therefore, in the wrong market, be partly paid by them. This is not an argument against the levy; it is an argument that the levy's effect cannot be read off its text.

Meanwhile, several states have enacted their own regimes, including fees linked to each transaction. This layering offers experiments from which lessons can be drawn, but it also invites a patchwork in which a platform operating nationally confronts different obligations in each jurisdiction, and in which a worker who crosses a state border may cross out of protection as well. Federal systems tolerate such variety because it can produce better ideas; whether it can also produce coherent protection for a mobile workforce is another matter entirely.

The sober assessment is that the Code has moved the debate from whether gig workers deserve protection to how protection is to be delivered, which is genuine progress and not the same as success. Its worth will be determined by details still being written: who registers, how benefits are funded and distributed, whether the cost lands where the law intends, and whether any provision addresses the algorithm that sits between the worker and the work. A framework that answers the first question while postponing the rest has built the doorway, not the house.

words.def: Very weak, slight or thin; lacking a firm basis.

words.def: Optimistic, especially in a difficult situation.

words.def: Unclear, vague or ill-defined.
words.ex: The policy goals were so nebulous that no one could measure success.

words.def: Deserving blame for a fault or wrong.

words.def: Understood or implied without being stated openly.

words.def: To make a bad situation better or more tolerable.

idioms.def: To change the rules or targets of something while it is in progress, usually unfairly.
idioms.ex: Just as we met the target, the manager moved the goalposts again.

idioms.def: Something that has both good and bad consequences.
idioms.ex: Automation is a double-edged sword: it raises output but also cuts jobs.

idioms.def: To understand a hidden or implied meaning that is not stated directly.
idioms.ex: If you read between the lines, the letter is really a polite warning.

idioms.def: In a risky or precarious situation.
idioms.ex: After two missed deadlines, the contractor was on thin ice.

idioms.idiom: Hit the nail on the head
idioms.def: To describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem.
idioms.ex: You hit the nail on the head when you blamed poor communication.

phrasalVerbs.def: To exclude something as a possibility.
phrasalVerbs.ex: The doctors ruled out an infection after the tests came back clear.

phrasalVerbs.def: To fail to happen or be completed.
phrasalVerbs.ex: The deal fell through at the last minute because of a funding gap.

phrasalVerbs.def: To explain or make up a particular proportion of something.
phrasalVerbs.ex: Exports account for nearly a third of the total output of the country.

phrasalVerbs.def: To use something such as experience or resources for a purpose.
phrasalVerbs.ex: The author draws on years of fieldwork to support her argument.

phrasalVerbs.def: To transfer something, such as a cost or message, to another person.
phrasalVerbs.ex: Retailers often pass on higher costs to their customers.

questions.question: The phrase "a ceiling disguised as a floor" in the second paragraph most plausibly implies that critics believe the scheme-based track
options: A) delivers benefits that fall below those already available to workers in the wider informal sector of the economy.
B) may become the most protection gig workers ever receive, even though it is presented as a minimum.
C) was drafted by the platforms themselves, and merely given legal form by a government that adopted their proposals.
D) promises employee status to every worker who registers, but only after a long and uncertain period of waiting.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option B
A floor is a minimum that can be built upon; a ceiling is a maximum. Critics fear that a scheme offered by application, capped in funding and separate from employee benefits will become the limit of what gig workers get, while being presented as a basic minimum.

Option A is wrong. The passage makes no comparison with informal-sector benefits. Unsupported.
Option C is wrong. The author attributes no role to platforms in drafting the Code. This is an unsupported claim.
Option D is wrong. The Code does not offer employee status at all; it deliberately creates a separate track. The option contradicts the paragraph.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author's objection to the platforms' defence of worker autonomy?
options: A) Workers who prize autonomy are mistaken about their own interests, since regular employment is always the better arrangement for them.
B) Algorithmic allocation of tasks is incompatible with any claim that platforms are merely marketplaces connecting independent parties.
C) Platforms deliberately mislead workers about the earnings they can expect from each task in order to keep them logged in.
D) Freedom to decline work is hollow if declining carries consequences that the worker cannot observe.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option D
The author argues autonomy is partly illusory because acceptance rates affect future allocation and the penalty for declining is invisible to the worker. So the freedom to decline exists in form but not in substance.

Option A is wrong. Too extreme. The author never says workers misjudge their interests or that employment is always better.
Option B is wrong. Too strong. The author questions how real the autonomy is but does not say the marketplace claim is impossible.
Option C is wrong. The passage mentions invisible penalties, not deliberate deception about earnings. Unsupported.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument in the fourth paragraph that platform-by-platform contributions suit a mobile workforce poorly?
options: A) Platforms with larger turnovers contribute more in absolute terms than smaller platforms, even where the rate of contribution is identical.
B) Workers who switch between several platforms report higher average hourly earnings than workers who remain with a single platform.
C) A central registry pools each worker's earnings across platforms and credits every contribution to a single account.
D) The algorithms that set surge prices on most platforms are not disclosed to the workers who depend on them for income.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option C
The author's worry is that fragmented income leaves each platform's contribution too thin to matter. If contributions are pooled in a single account per worker, the fragmentation problem largely disappears, which directly weakens the argument.

Option A is wrong. Larger platforms paying more in absolute terms says nothing about whether one worker's benefits are fragmented across platforms.
Option B is wrong. Higher earnings for platform-switchers do not bear on whether contributions can be consolidated; this is irrelevant to portability.
Option D is wrong. Non-disclosure of surge algorithms relates to the third paragraph's concern with control, not to the fragmentation of contributions.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred from the discussion of incidence in the fifth paragraph?
options: A) Identical contribution rates can leave workers worse off in some markets than in others, depending on how competitive the market is.
B) Platforms in concentrated markets will necessarily absorb the whole cost of the levy rather than pass any part of it on to customers.
C) The levy ought to be abandoned, because in practice it is likely to be paid for by the very workers it was meant to protect.
D) Customers in markets where price sensitivity is high are the party most exposed to the burden of the levy once it takes effect.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option A
The paragraph says incidence depends on market structure: where competition and price sensitivity are high, the burden can drift to workers; where a few firms dominate, they may absorb or pass on the cost at will. The same levy therefore has different effects in different markets.

Option B is wrong. Too strong. The author says dominant firms may absorb the cost or pass it on at will, not that they necessarily absorb it all.
Option C is wrong. The author expressly says this is not an argument against the levy, only that its effect cannot be read off its text.
Option D is wrong. Reversed. High price sensitivity limits platforms' ability to raise prices, which pushes the burden away from customers and towards workers.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the state-level regimes discussed in the sixth paragraph is best described as
options: A) firm disapproval, since they duplicate obligations and place unreasonable burdens on any platform that operates across the country.
B) qualified approval: it values the experimentation they allow but doubts that it yields coherent protection.
C) indifference, since the paragraph treats the effects as a matter for platforms to resolve rather than something affecting workers.
D) enthusiastic endorsement, since the paragraph holds that federal systems generate better ideas than centralised systems ever can.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option B
The author grants that layering offers experiments from which lessons can be drawn, then raises the risk of a patchwork and says whether it produces coherent protection is another matter entirely. That is approval with reservations.

Option A is wrong. The author notes the patchwork risk but also credits the benefits of experimentation, so disapproval is too strong.
Option C is wrong. The paragraph explicitly concerns workers who may cross out of protection, so it cannot be called indifferent to them.
Option D is wrong. The author says variety can produce better ideas but never claims that federal systems are better than centralised ones; the doubt about coherence rules out enthusiasm.

questions.question: The metaphor "built the doorway, not the house" in the final paragraph suggests that the author believes the Code
options: A) is symbolically important but legally ineffective, since it creates no enforceable obligations on any aggregator.
B) will be overtaken by state legislation that supplies the substantive benefits which the central framework lacks.
C) creates a precondition for real protection without yet supplying the substance that would make it meaningful.
D) has taken a first step that the author expects aggregators to resist strongly in the courts over the coming years.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: Option C
A doorway is an entry point, not a dwelling. The author says the Code answers whether gig workers deserve protection while postponing who registers, how benefits are funded and whether costs land fairly. It has opened the way but not yet delivered the protection.

Option A is wrong. The Code does create obligations, since aggregators may be required to contribute; the author calls the progress genuine.
Option B is wrong. The author does not predict that state laws will supply the missing substance; the missing details are those of the central framework.
Option D is wrong. Litigation by aggregators is never mentioned. The prediction is unsupported.

title: Linguistic Relativity, Untranslatability, and the Limits of Thought
