passage:
The idea that the language a person speaks shapes the thoughts that person can think has had a long and uneven career. In its strongest form, associated with the linguists Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, it holds that grammar and vocabulary set the boundaries of cognition: speakers of a language that lacks a word or grammatical category for a concept cannot grasp it, or grasp it only dimly. This claim, known as linguistic determinism, has been abandoned by most researchers, partly because it is hard to square with translation itself. If a concept were unthinkable without a word for it, no description of that concept in another language could make it intelligible, yet such descriptions routinely do. The weaker thesis, linguistic relativity, which says that language influences habitual attention and memory without fixing what is thinkable, has nonetheless enjoyed a revival in recent decades, supported by experiment rather than anecdote.

The experimental case is modest but suggestive. Speakers of Russian, which has separate basic terms for lighter and darker blues, tell apart shades that straddle the boundary slightly faster than English speakers, who have a single term. Speakers of some Aboriginal Australian languages, which describe location by compass direction instead of left and right, keep track of orientation in unfamiliar surroundings and even indoors, and arrange cards depicting a sequence from east to west whichever way they face. Such results are real, but they invite two readings. On one, language restructures perception. On the other, speakers practise a skill their communities value, and the vocabulary is a symptom of that practice rather than its cause. The experiments alone cannot separate the readings, because a community's language and its way of life vary together.

A subtler difficulty concerns what the experiments actually show. The differences appear chiefly in speed, in tasks demanding fine discrimination or memory, and they shrink or vanish when participants must repeat a meaningless string of digits while performing the task, which occupies their verbal resources. This suggests that language acts as a tool consulted during a task rather than a lens fixed over perception, and a tool can be put down. The distinction matters for the grander claims drawn from the research, since an effect that disappears when verbal resources are busy cannot be the permanent reshaping of the mind that popular accounts announce. Advocates reply that habitual tools change their users; a pianist's hands differ from a typist's. The effect on thought may be real without being deep, but where habit ends and structure begins is itself unclear.

Translation enters the debate from the opposite direction. The claim that certain words are untranslatable, such as the Portuguese saudade or the German Schadenfreude, is repeated so often that it has acquired the status of common knowledge. But it conflates the absence of a single word with the absence of a concept. English has no single word for Schadenfreude, yet English speakers need little persuading that pleasure at another's misfortune exists, and a phrase of five words conveys it. What translation loses is seldom the concept; it is the connotation, rhythm and register that the word carries in its home language. That loss is real, but it is cultural rather than cognitive. The ease of paraphrase can nevertheless be overstated: a concept that needs a sentence each time it is mentioned will be mentioned less, and perhaps thought about less. This returns us, by another route, to relativity of the weak sort, in which language shapes not what can be thought but what is convenient to think.

There is a further twist in the way the debate has been conducted. Researchers have mostly studied differences between languages in domains where differences can be measured, such as colour, space, number and grammatical gender, and these are domains where the physical world supplies a common standard against which responses can be tested. Where a language might shape thought about matters lacking an external standard, such as morality, kinship or the self, there is no neutral yardstick, and the absence of evidence of influence is not evidence of its absence. The research programme thus finds effects where they can be measured and falls silent where they might matter most. This is an instance of a familiar pattern, in which a field's methods determine its findings by determining what it is able to see.

Studies of grammatical gender illustrate the problem. German speakers, for whom the word for bridge is feminine, are reported to describe bridges as elegant or slender, while Spanish speakers, for whom it is masculine, choose words such as strong or sturdy. But these results come largely from tasks in which participants used the language in question, so the effect may reflect only the activation of gendered associations at the moment of speaking, not any lasting difference in how bridges are seen. When similar tasks are run with participants verbally occupied, the pattern weakens. Whether the finding counts as evidence for relativity therefore depends on whether thinking at the moment of speech counts as thinking at all. Some scholars answer that it does, arguing that every language obliges its speakers to attend to particular features of the world whenever they speak, such as time, gender or the source of one's knowledge, and that this constant obligation, though confined to speech, is a real form of influence.

The most defensible conclusion may be that the question as usually posed, whether language shapes thought, yes or no, is badly formed. Language is not a single thing acting on a single mind. It supplies categories that are cheap to use, directs attention at moments of speech, and records the accumulated practices of a community, and it can do each of these without limiting anyone's capacity to think otherwise. The strong claim is false, the weak claim is true but unremarkable, and what remains interesting lies in between: which habits of attention are induced by which grammatical obligations, how durable they are, and whether they matter outside the laboratory. The danger is twofold. The moral appeal of the strong claim, which flatters the diversity of human cultures by making them mutually unintelligible, tempts writers to keep it, while the modest evidence for the weak claim tempts sceptics to dismiss it altogether. Both errors misdescribe what has been found.

questions.question: Which of the following findings would most seriously challenge the 'tool' interpretation of the colour-discrimination results described in paragraph 3?
options: A) The faster discrimination across the colour boundary persists undiminished even while participants are repeating a string of digits throughout the whole task.
B) The faster discrimination appears only in tasks where participants are asked to name the shades aloud before they respond, and nowhere else in the experiment.
C) The faster discrimination is larger in tasks that require participants to hold the shades in memory for several seconds than in tasks requiring immediate comparison.
D) Speakers who learn the language later in life show the same faster discrimination as speakers who acquired it in early childhood, according to follow-up studies.
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option A is Correct: The 'tool' reading says language is consulted during the task, so occupying verbal resources should erase the effect (as paragraph 3 reports). If the effect survives verbal interference, language is not being consulted as a removable tool, and the interpretation is damaged.

• Why Option B is Wrong: Appearing only when participants name the shades aloud is exactly what the tool reading predicts, since naming means consulting language. It supports rather than challenges the reading.

• Why Option C is Wrong: A larger effect in memory tasks is consistent with a tool used during the task (the passage says differences appear in tasks demanding fine discrimination or memory); it does not separate the two readings.

• Why Option D is Wrong: Equal effects for late and early learners say nothing about whether the effect depends on verbal resources during the task, so the tool reading is untouched.

💡 Approach: To weaken an interpretation, find its distinctive prediction (effect vanishes under verbal interference) and look for the finding that violates it. Options that merely fit or are neutral are traps.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the sentence beginning 'The ease of paraphrase can nevertheless be overstated' serves chiefly to:
options: A) retract the claim that translation loses connotation and register rather than concepts, so that untranslatable words are admitted to be real after all
B) show that translators are prone to errors that would be avoided if they gave up paraphrase in favour of single-word equivalents in all circumstances
C) prove that English speakers think less often about pleasure at another's misfortune because their language has no single word for it
D) concede that being able to paraphrase a concept does not rule out a weak influence of language on what it is convenient to think about
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option D is Correct: The author has just argued that concepts survive translation. The 'nevertheless' sentence concedes a limit: a concept needing a whole sentence is mentioned, and perhaps thought of, less often, which is the weak form of relativity (what is convenient to think), not an inability to think.

• Why Option A is Wrong: The author does not retract the claim; paragraph 4 still says the loss is 'cultural rather than cognitive' and that the concept itself is seldom lost.

• Why Option B is Wrong: Nothing in the paragraph criticises translators or recommends single-word equivalents; this introduces an unrelated claim.

• Why Option C is Wrong: 'Prove' is far too strong: the author says 'perhaps thought about less', a possibility, and the English example was used earlier to show English speakers do grasp the idea.

💡 Approach: Function-of-a-sentence questions: read the sentence before it and the sentence after it. The word 'nevertheless' signals a concession, not a reversal of the author's main point.

questions.question: The author states that 'the absence of evidence of influence is not evidence of its absence' (paragraph 5) in order to argue that:
options: A) language must be shaping thought about morality, kinship and the self, because researchers have not been able to demonstrate otherwise
B) the physical world supplies no common standard, which is why experiments on colour, space and number should be disregarded altogether
C) the lack of measured effects in domains such as morality reflects a limit of method, not a finding that language has no influence there
D) researchers have deliberately avoided domains where language might have the largest effects in order to protect their favoured conclusions
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option C is Correct: The author says that where there is no external yardstick, no measured influence cannot be read as no influence. The silence of the research programme there reflects what its methods can see.

• Why Option A is Wrong: This turns the author's point into its opposite: it treats absence of evidence as evidence of presence. The author only denies that absence of evidence shows absence.

• Why Option B is Wrong: The author says the physical world supplies a standard in those domains, which makes them measurable; nothing suggests disregarding such experiments.

• Why Option D is Wrong: The passage attributes the pattern to methods determining what a field can see, not to deliberate avoidance or motives.

💡 Approach: Distinguish 'cannot conclude absence' from 'conclude presence'. Distractors either flip the logic or add a motive the author never alleges.

questions.question: The author's remark that 'a field's methods determine its findings by determining what it is able to see' is most closely paralleled by which of the following?
options: A) A detective who suspects the nearest neighbour because that neighbour has the weakest alibi of everyone living on the street
B) A search party that combs only the lit meadow because the dark forest is hard to search, then reports that the missing child is not nearby
C) A cartographer who leaves unsurveyed regions blank and labels them 'unknown' on the published map so that readers are not misled
D) A chemist who repeats an experiment ten times, obtains the same result each time, and publishes it with the full procedure attached for others
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option B is Correct: The search party's method (search only where it is easy to look) determines its finding (child not nearby), and the silence about the forest is mistaken for absence. This mirrors a field that finds effects only where they can be measured and treats silence elsewhere as a finding.

• Why Option A is Wrong: The detective reasons from a weak alibi, which is a (perhaps poor) clue about guilt; no limitation of method is mistaken for a finding.

• Why Option C is Wrong: The cartographer is careful: unsurveyed regions are explicitly marked unknown. This is the opposite of confusing a limit of method with a finding.

• Why Option D is Wrong: Replication under the same procedure is a sound practice and involves no blindness caused by the method.

💡 Approach: For parallel-reasoning questions, state the abstract structure first: 'method limits what is seen, and the limit is mistaken for a result'. Then reject options with only surface similarity (searching, mapping, experiments).

questions.question: All of the following can be inferred from the passage EXCEPT:
options: A) Speakers of a language with more colour terms outperform speakers of other languages in every colour-discrimination task, whatever else they are doing.
B) The experimental findings on compass-direction languages can be explained without assuming that language restructures perception, since cultural practice may drive both.
C) Even if grammatical obligations influence thinking only at the moment of speaking, some scholars would still count this as a genuine form of linguistic influence.
D) The popularity of the strong claim owes something to its flattering picture of cultural diversity, according to the author, not simply to the strength of evidence.
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option A is Correct: The passage says differences shrink or vanish when participants are verbally occupied (paragraph 3) and are mainly differences in speed, so 'every task, whatever else they are doing' contradicts it. This is the statement that cannot be inferred.

• Why Option B is Wrong: Paragraph 2 gives exactly this alternative reading: practice of a valued skill may cause both the vocabulary and the behaviour.

• Why Option C is Wrong: Paragraph 6 reports that some scholars argue the constant obligation to attend to certain features, though confined to speech, is a real form of influence.

• Why Option D is Wrong: Paragraph 7 says the strong claim's moral appeal, flattering cultural diversity, tempts writers to keep it.

💡 Approach: In EXCEPT questions three options are supported and one is not. Check each against a specific paragraph; the odd one out is usually an absolute ('every', 'whatever') that the text qualifies.

questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the author's overall position?
options: A) Linguistic determinism has been refuted by experiment, and relativity, which has replaced it, shows that language deeply and permanently restructures thought in each speaker
B) Research on language and thought is so limited by its methods and so open to rival explanations that it has taught us nothing and should be set aside
C) Translation shows that concepts cross languages freely, so that language has no influence on thought and experimental claims to the contrary are mistaken
D) The strong claim is false and the weak claim modest; the productive question concerns which specific habits of attention language induces and how durable they are
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option D is Correct: Paragraph 7 states that the strong claim is false, the weak claim true but unremarkable, and what remains interesting are the specific habits induced by grammatical obligations and their durability and significance.

• Why Option A is Wrong: Determinism is rejected partly on grounds of translation, not 'refuted by experiment', and the author denies that the effects are deep or permanent (the 'tool' argument).

• Why Option B is Wrong: The author calls the evidence modest but real, and concludes that the weak claim is true and that sceptics who dismiss it altogether commit an error.

• Why Option C is Wrong: The author says the loss in translation is cultural and allows that language may still influence what is convenient to think; 'no influence' is the sceptics' error the author warns against.

💡 Approach: Summary questions: the correct option reflects both halves of the author's balanced conclusion. Options that go to either extreme (deep and permanent, or nothing at all) are typical traps.

title: Eyewitness Memory, Confidence, and the Courtroom Problem of Certainty

words.def: A tendency to believe things too readily.
words.ex: The scam relied on the credulity of its victims.

words.def: Rebuilding something from parts or fragments rather than reproducing it exactly.
words.ex: Memory is reconstructive, not a recording.

words.def: Of secondary importance; on the edge of the main focus.

words.ex: Leading questions can contaminate a witness’s account.

words.def: To clear someone of blame or a criminal charge.

words.def: The tendency to make mistakes or be wrong.
words.ex: The fallibility of memory is well documented.

words.def: To increase something beyond its true or proper size.

idioms.idiom: Beyond a shadow of a doubt

idioms.ex: The prosecution claimed guilt beyond a shadow of a doubt.

idioms.idiom: Take with a pinch of salt
idioms.def: To treat a claim with some scepticism.
idioms.ex: Take the witness’s confidence with a pinch of salt.

idioms.def: To have both good and bad effects.
idioms.ex: Stricter procedures can cut both ways.

idioms.def: To change a balance of opinion or outcome decisively.
idioms.ex: One confident witness can tip the scales.

idioms.def: Past events are easier to understand once they are known.
idioms.ex: Hindsight is twenty-twenty, but the warning signs were there.

phrasalVerbs.def: To consider the merits of something carefully.
phrasalVerbs.ex: Jurors must weigh up all the evidence.

phrasalVerbs.def: To choose one person or thing from a group.
phrasalVerbs.ex: The witness singled out the man in the second row.

phrasalVerbs.def: To give a particular impression.
phrasalVerbs.ex: Confident witnesses come across as reliable.

phrasalVerbs.def: To support or confirm something.
phrasalVerbs.ex: DNA evidence backed up his alibi.

phrasalVerbs.def: To prove to be the case in the end.
phrasalVerbs.ex: The identification turned out to be mistaken.

passage:
Few forms of evidence move a jury as powerfully as a witness who points at the defendant and says, “That is the man.” Courts have relied on such testimony for centuries, on the intuition that memory works like a recording: events are stored and, with sufficient effort, replayed. Psychological research over the past half-century has undermined this picture. Remembering is reconstructive: the mind stores fragments and rebuilds an episode at recall, filling gaps with expectation, inference and information acquired afterwards. A reconstruction can be vivid, detailed and confidently held while being wrong in ways the rememberer cannot detect, which is precisely what makes it dangerous in a courtroom. The danger is compounded by the fact that the witness is usually sincere: a liar can be cross-examined, but a sincere witness who is mistaken has no reason to doubt himself, and the court has little to go on except his manner.

The best-known demonstrations concern suggestion. In classic experiments, participants who watched film of a traffic accident gave higher speed estimates when asked how fast the cars were going when they “smashed” into each other than when the verb was “hit”, and a week later were more likely to report having seen broken glass that was not in the film. This “misinformation effect” shows that post-event information can be absorbed into memory, so that a later question becomes part of the remembered event. The legal implications are plain: every interview, every photograph shown and every conversation with other witnesses may contaminate the evidence before it reaches the courtroom. Yet the reach of these findings is easy to overstate. Many of the experiments involve peripheral details, such as a piece of glass or a street sign, rather than central ones such as a face, and contamination appears weakest for what a witness attended to most closely.

The most contested question is the relationship between confidence and accuracy. For decades, reviews concluded that a witness’s confidence in an identification is a poor guide to its accuracy, and jurors, who find confident witnesses more persuasive, were accused of being systematically misled. More recent work qualifies this. When an identification is made at the first attempt, from a fair lineup, by a witness not yet contaminated by suggestion, high confidence is a strong indicator of accuracy. The difficulty is that these conditions are seldom met by the time a case is heard. At trial, confidence has often been inflated by feedback, repeated questioning and the simple act of having committed to a choice, while accuracy, of course, has not changed. Confidence is thus a good signal when first recorded under clean conditions and a poor one when displayed in court; the same word describes two different measurements.

Procedural reform has been the main practical response. Double-blind lineups, in which the officer administering the lineup does not know which person is the suspect, remove the unintentional cues that can steer a witness. Fillers who match the witness’s description, clear warnings that the culprit may not be present, and immediate recording of the witness’s confidence are cheap changes that most researchers endorse. Other reforms are less settled. Whether suspects should be shown simultaneously or one at a time was long debated: sequential presentation appeared to reduce false identifications, but later analyses suggested that it also reduces correct ones, so the apparent gain in caution may be a shift in willingness to choose rather than an improvement in discrimination. A reform that merely makes witnesses more reluctant to identify anyone will reduce mistaken convictions only by also reducing correct ones, and whether that trade is desirable is a question of values, not of psychology.

Critics raise a different objection to the whole project: laboratory findings, obtained from students watching staged events with nothing at stake, cannot be transferred to real witnesses who are frightened, motivated and questioned about events of real consequence. The objection has force, since stress and the presence of a weapon, which draws attention away from the face, are hard to reproduce ethically. But its direction is not obvious. Some real-world evidence, notably the many convictions later overturned by DNA analysis in which a mistaken identification played a part and which have prompted many legal systems to revisit their procedures, suggests that errors in the field can be at least as serious as errors in the laboratory. One cannot, however, treat these exonerations as a representative sample: they are cases in which biological evidence happened to survive, and they reveal that identifications can be wrong, not how often they typically are.

A further complication lies in what the law asks of the research. Courts must decide whether this identification, by this witness, is reliable, whereas psychology speaks in probabilities about classes of witnesses under classes of conditions. Expert testimony on memory is meant to bridge the gap, but it can only describe what tends to happen; it cannot say what happened here. Some judges therefore exclude it as unhelpful, reasoning that jurors need no instruction in the fallibility of memory. The research suggests the reverse: jurors’ intuitions about memory are often inaccurate, and in particular they tend to believe that confidence and accuracy track each other closely, when the relation depends on conditions they cannot see. Yet an expert who explains this risks swinging the jury from excessive credulity to excessive scepticism, which is a distortion of its own.

The deepest lesson may concern the structure of the problem. Memory evidence differs from a fingerprint in that the witness is both the instrument and the reporter: the same mind that records the event also decides how sure to be, and the certainty it reports is shaped by everything that happens afterwards. Legal systems cannot dispense with witnesses, since many crimes leave no other trace. The realistic goal is therefore not to abolish testimony but to treat it as evidence whose weight depends on how it was collected, and to preserve the earliest, cleanest record of it. A procedure that does so makes honest witnesses more useful; one that does not makes them more dangerous, however sincere they are.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author’s claim that confidence displayed at trial is a poor guide to accuracy?
options: A) Jurors who hear confident witnesses are more likely to convict than jurors who hear hesitant witnesses, even when other evidence in the two cases is identical.
B) Witnesses who are given positive feedback after identifying a suspect report higher confidence at trial than witnesses who receive no feedback after the lineup.
C) Where a first identification was made under clean conditions, confidence at trial is almost always the same as the confidence first recorded.
D) Confidence at trial is higher for witnesses who were questioned repeatedly before the hearing than for witnesses who were questioned only once beforehand.
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option C is Correct: The author’s reasoning is that trial confidence is inflated by feedback and repeated questioning while accuracy does not change. If trial confidence in fact matches the confidence first recorded under clean conditions, it carries the same information as that reliable early signal, so the claim is undermined.

• Why Option A is Wrong: This concerns how jurors respond to confidence, not whether confidence tracks accuracy, so it neither weakens nor strengthens the claim.

• Why Option B is Wrong: This supports the author: feedback inflates confidence without improving accuracy.

• Why Option D is Wrong: This too supports the author, since repeated questioning is named as a source of inflated confidence.

💡 Approach: To weaken, attack the mechanism the author gives (inflation between the first identification and trial). Options that repeat or fit the mechanism are strengtheners, and juror behaviour is irrelevant to the accuracy question.

questions.question: The author notes that sequential lineups may reduce correct identifications as well as false ones (paragraph 4) in order to:
options: A) prove that sequential lineups should be abandoned in favour of simultaneous lineups in every jurisdiction that currently permits them to be used
B) show that an apparent gain in caution may be a mere shift in willingness to choose, so that choosing between reforms is a matter of values
C) argue that psychology has no useful contribution to make to the design of police procedures concerning the identification of suspects at all
D) suggest that double-blind administration, unlike sequential presentation, should be regarded as an unsettled reform among researchers
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option B is Correct: The author says the apparent gain may be a shift in willingness to choose rather than better discrimination, and that whether the trade between mistaken and correct identifications is desirable is a question of values, not of psychology.

• Why Option A is Wrong: The author never recommends abandoning sequential lineups; the point is about interpreting their effect.

• Why Option C is Wrong: The author credits psychology with several uncontroversial reforms (double-blind lineups, fillers, warnings); the claim is only that one trade-off is evaluative.

• Why Option D is Wrong: Double-blind administration is listed among the reforms most researchers endorse, so it is not unsettled; the option inverts the paragraph.

💡 Approach: Purpose questions: find the point the author draws immediately after the fact. Here it is the last sentence of the paragraph.

questions.question: The author cautions against treating DNA exonerations as a representative sample. Which of the following conclusions is therefore best supported?
options: A) Mistaken identifications are rare in real cases, since most convictions that rest on them are never overturned by any later analysis
B) Laboratory findings about misidentification should be set aside in favour of the evidence from real cases in which biological material survived
C) Errors in the field are likely to be less serious than errors in the laboratory, since the exonerations involve only a small number of cases
D) The exonerations show that identifications can be wrong in real cases, but they do not indicate how often identifications are wrong in general
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option D is Correct: The author says the exonerations come from cases in which biological evidence happened to survive, and that they reveal that identifications can be wrong, not how often they typically are.

• Why Option A is Wrong: Unexamined convictions may include many errors; absence of overturning is not evidence of accuracy. The author draws no such conclusion.

• Why Option B is Wrong: The author uses the exonerations to question the critics’ objection, not to discard laboratory research; the paragraph defends the research’s relevance.

• Why Option C is Wrong: The author says errors in the field can be at least as serious as in the laboratory; the small number of cases is not claimed to show less serious errors.

💡 Approach: A non-representative sample supports existence claims ('can happen') but not frequency claims ('how often'). Look for the option that respects that limit.

questions.question: The author’s point that a reform which merely makes witnesses more reluctant to identify anyone reduces mistaken convictions only by also reducing correct ones is most closely paralleled by:
options: A) A smoke alarm made less sensitive so that it stops sounding for burnt toast, but which now also fails in some real fires
B) A teacher who marks all examinations twice and awards the average, which reduces the effect of any single careless marker in the school
C) A bank that checks the identity of every customer in person, which prevents fraud and also reassures honest customers
D) A pharmacist who discontinues a medicine because a cheaper and equally effective drug has become available on the market
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option A is Correct: Lowering the willingness to respond cuts false alarms and misses together: it trades errors of one kind for errors of another, which is the structure of the lineup point.

• Why Option B is Wrong: Double marking reduces random error without trading one error for another.

• Why Option C is Wrong: Checking identity reduces fraud without any compensating loss of correct outcomes; it is a pure gain.

• Why Option D is Wrong: Replacing a medicine with an equal and cheaper one involves no trade-off between two kinds of error.

💡 Approach: Extract the structure first: a shift in threshold that lowers one error and raises another. Then reject options where both outcomes improve or there is no error trade-off.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the misinformation effect from the passage?
options: A) It proves that eyewitnesses cannot be trusted about any detail of an event after they have been questioned about it by officials
B) It is confined to laboratory settings, because real witnesses are too frightened and too motivated to be influenced by later questions
C) Its practical importance depends in part on whether the details affected are peripheral to what the witness attended to
D) It has been shown to be weakest for suspects’ faces, since faces are always attended to more closely than anything else
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option C is Correct: The author says many experiments involve peripheral details and that contamination appears weakest for what the witness attended to most closely, so how far the effect matters depends on the kind of detail.

• Why Option A is Wrong: 'Proves', 'cannot be trusted about any detail' overstate; the author warns the findings are easy to overstate.

• Why Option B is Wrong: The objection about laboratory settings is raised by critics, and the author doubts its direction rather than endorsing it.

• Why Option D is Wrong: The passage says contamination is weakest for what was attended to most closely and mentions faces as a central detail, but 'always attended to more closely than anything else' and 'shown to be weakest for faces' go beyond the text.

💡 Approach: Prefer the option that carries the same qualification the passage does ('in part', 'depends'). Absolutes ('proves', 'always', 'any') are usually the trap.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that expert testimony on memory:
options: A) should be excluded because jurors already understand that memory is fallible and need no instruction from specialists in psychology
B) is justified by mistaken juror intuitions but must be given carefully, lest credulity be replaced by an equally distorting scepticism
C) can tell the court whether a particular witness’s identification in the case at hand is accurate, because it is based on scientific research
D) is unnecessary once reforms such as double-blind lineups have been adopted, since these remove the causes of misidentification
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option B is Correct: Paragraph 6 says jurors’ intuitions are often inaccurate (supporting such testimony) but that an expert risks swinging the jury from credulity to scepticism, a distortion of its own.

• Why Option A is Wrong: This is the reasoning of the judges mentioned, which the author says the research contradicts.

• Why Option C is Wrong: The author says expert testimony can only describe what tends to happen and cannot say what happened here.

• Why Option D is Wrong: Reforms improve the collection of evidence but do not remove juror misconceptions; the author nowhere says they make expert testimony unnecessary.

💡 Approach: When the author reports a view and then says 'the research suggests the reverse', the reported view is a distractor. The correct option contains both the support and the caveat.

title: Density, Preservation, and the Politics of Who Gets to Live in the City

passage:
Cities exist because people and firms gain from proximity. Economists call these gains agglomeration economies and trace them to three sources: shared inputs, such as ports and specialised suppliers, which are cheaper to maintain for many firms than for a few; a deep labour market, in which workers and employers find better matches; and knowledge spillovers, in which ideas pass between people who meet. These forces help explain why wages in large cities exceed those in small ones even after adjusting for differences in workers’ skills, and why the premium has persisted despite the falling cost of transporting goods and, more recently, of transmitting information. If communications technology were a perfect substitute for proximity, cities would have emptied. They did not, which suggests that some of what proximity provides cannot be sent through a wire.

The benefits, however, come with costs, and the costs are often borne by people other than those who enjoy the benefits. Density raises land prices; congestion slows movement; and crowded places transmit disease more readily, a fact that earlier centuries of epidemics made plain and that recent experience restored to public attention. Whether a given city is too dense or too sparse is therefore not a question with a single answer. Economists describe the optimum as the point at which the marginal benefit of one more resident equals the marginal cost, but neither marginal quantity is observed directly, and both change as technology and tastes change. A level of density that was ruinous in a city of coal fires and horse-drawn traffic may be benign in one of electric trains.

Planning in the twentieth century treated these costs as the central problem. Modernist planners, impressed by the squalor of industrial slums, proposed to separate functions, with housing here, work there and recreation elsewhere, and to reduce density through towers set in open space and roads built for cars. Their critics, most famously the writer Jane Jacobs, argued that this treated a city as a machine to be designed rather than an organism that grows. Lively streets, she said, depend on mixed uses, short blocks, buildings of different ages and enough people to keep the pavement in use at all hours; the very features that planners regarded as disorder produced the informal surveillance that made streets safe and the diversity that made them interesting. The argument was empirical as much as aesthetic, and history gave it considerable support: many of the large projects that embodied the modernist ideal deteriorated, and some were demolished within decades.

Yet the Jacobs view, in its popular form, has a blind spot of its own. It tends to treat the existing fabric of a lively neighbourhood as something to be preserved, and preservation has a price. When a desirable district restricts new construction, whether through height limits, minimum lot sizes or lengthy approval procedures, the demand to live there does not disappear; it expresses itself in higher rents, and those who can pay them displace those who cannot. The neighbourhood is preserved in form while being transformed in population. Defenders of tight controls reply that unrestricted building would destroy the very qualities that made the place attractive, and that existing residents have legitimate claims to the neighbourhood they helped create. Both points have weight. But the first quietly assumes that new construction must resemble the worst of the past, and the second treats the interests of incumbents as decisive without asking about the interests of those who are not yet residents and therefore have no vote.

This last observation points to the political structure of the problem. The costs of new housing are concentrated and visible: construction noise, shadows, more traffic on a particular street. The benefits are diffuse and mostly invisible: slightly lower rents across a whole metropolitan area, enjoyed by people who cannot know that they have benefited. Where decisions on land use are made at the most local level, the concentrated losers are better organised than the diffuse winners, and the result is predictable. Some economists therefore favour moving authority upward, to regional or national governments, which weigh benefits that local bodies ignore. Others reply that this solves the political problem at the price of a knowledge problem: local residents know things about their streets that distant authorities do not, and a rule applied everywhere may suit nowhere.

Empirical evidence on the effect of new supply is mixed and often misread. Studies of new buildings have found that adding market-rate housing in a neighbourhood tends to reduce rents in nearby older buildings relative to comparable areas where nothing was built, which is consistent with simple supply and demand. But a finding that rents are lower than they would otherwise have been is a counterfactual claim, and counterfactuals are hard to see: a resident watching rents rise in a district where building has begun may reasonably conclude that building caused the rise, when it may only have been slower than the demand that prompted it. This asymmetry between what is seen and what is not seen gives each side in the debate material for its case. Those who oppose building point to the rent increases they can see; those who favour it point to the increases that did not occur, which no one can see.

The better conclusion is that density is neither a virtue nor a vice, but a variable whose value depends on what accompanies it. Dense districts with good transport, a mix of uses and adequate public services can be both productive and pleasant; dense districts without them are crowded and unhealthy. Equally, low density protects some people at the expense of others, a fact its defenders often leave unstated. A city that treats all change as a threat will in time become a museum, admired by visitors and unaffordable to workers; one that treats all change as progress will forget what made it worth living in. Policy should be judged by whom it asks to bear costs and whom it allows to share the gains.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the inference in paragraph 1 that some of what proximity provides cannot be sent through a wire?
options: A) The wage premium in large cities is larger for workers in occupations that require frequent face-to-face meetings with clients than for other workers.
B) Surveys of firms show that managers in large cities rate chance meetings with workers from other firms as a major source of new ideas.
C) Ports and specialised suppliers remain concentrated in large cities because the equipment they use is too costly to be duplicated in many places.
D) Most firms remain in large cities only because leases and relocation costs make leaving expensive, and many are moving out as their leases expire.
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option D is Correct: The inference is that cities did not empty because proximity offers something transmission cannot. If firms stay only because exit is costly and are leaving as soon as costs lapse, their persistence no longer shows that proximity provides something irreplaceable, so the inference is weakened.

• Why Option A is Wrong: A larger premium for face-to-face occupations supports the idea that some benefits need presence.

• Why Option B is Wrong: Chance meetings as a source of ideas is the knowledge-spillover channel, which supports the inference.

• Why Option C is Wrong: This explains concentration through a shared-input channel that does not depend on communications at all; it neither supports nor undermines the claim about what cannot be sent through a wire.

💡 Approach: To weaken an inference, offer an alternative explanation for the observed fact. Here the fact is that cities did not empty; the alternative is that firms are merely locked in.

questions.question: The author observes that ‘neither marginal quantity is observed directly’ (paragraph 2) in order to suggest that:
options: A) the economists’ notion of an optimum density is meaningless and should be replaced by rules based on the preferences of planners
B) cities should aim for the lowest feasible density, since the costs of crowding are known to exceed the benefits of proximity
C) the best level of density cannot be read off from a simple formula and is likely to differ across places and times
D) technology has made the marginal costs of density negligible, so that cities no longer need to consider the question of limits
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option C is Correct: Because neither the marginal benefit nor marginal cost is observed directly, and both change with technology and tastes, the optimum is hard to determine and varies, as the coal-and-horses versus electric-trains example illustrates.

• Why Option A is Wrong: The author uses the optimum concept and does not call it meaningless; the difficulty is measuring it.

• Why Option B is Wrong: The paragraph says the answer is not single and that density can be benign; it does not say costs are known to exceed benefits.

• Why Option D is Wrong: The author says costs remain and can differ with technology; they are not said to be negligible.

💡 Approach: Match the claim to the specific difficulty mentioned: unobservable and changing quantities mean no fixed answer. Extreme options (always minimise, always ignore) are typical traps.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author’s attitude to the view associated with Jane Jacobs?
options: A) Respectful of its empirical force, but critical of a popular version that neglects the costs of preserving a neighbourhood as it is
B) Enthusiastic in endorsing it, since the author holds that the preservation of existing neighbourhoods serves the interests of all residents
C) Dismissive of it as a purely aesthetic preference that was disproved by the experience of the large modernist housing projects
D) Neutral, since the author reports the view and the objections to it without suggesting that either side has made a valid point
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option A is Correct: Paragraph 3 says the argument was empirical and received considerable support from history; paragraph 4 says its popular form has a blind spot, since preservation has a price in higher rents and displacement.

• Why Option B is Wrong: The author argues that preservation can displace poorer residents, so it does not serve all residents.

• Why Option C is Wrong: The author says the argument was empirical as much as aesthetic, and that history supported it; the modernist projects, not the Jacobs view, are said to have deteriorated.

• Why Option D is Wrong: The author states that the view has a blind spot and that both sides in the next debate have weight, so the attitude is not neutral.

💡 Approach: Attitude questions: find both the praise and the criticism. The correct option is usually the balanced one that matches each.

questions.question: The author’s criticism of the defenders’ second reply (that existing residents have legitimate claims) is that it:
options: A) denies that residents have any claim to the neighbourhood they helped to create, and so misrepresents their interests
B) treats incumbents’ interests as decisive while ignoring prospective residents, who have no vote in the matter
C) assumes that unrestricted building would necessarily destroy the character of the neighbourhood in which it takes place
D) overlooks that approval procedures for new construction are often lengthy and add to the cost of every new unit built
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option B is Correct: The author says the second point 'treats the interests of incumbents as decisive without asking about the interests of those who are not yet residents and therefore have no vote'.

• Why Option A is Wrong: The author concedes both points have weight and does not deny residents’ claims.

• Why Option C is Wrong: This is the first reply (unrestricted building would destroy qualities), which the author criticises for a different assumption.

• Why Option D is Wrong: The cost of approval procedures is mentioned in the paragraph, but not as a criticism of the second reply.

💡 Approach: The author criticises the first and second replies differently. Keep track of which sentence belongs to which point.

questions.question: The author’s point about ‘what is seen and what is not seen’ in the debate over rents is most closely paralleled by:
options: A) A coach who selects the fastest runners for a relay team and then claims all the credit for the team’s win in the national final
B) A student who studies only the topics that appear on the syllabus and omits all others, and therefore passes the examination
C) A shopkeeper who discounts every item in the shop in the belief that a sale will bring in more customers than any other measure could in the town
D) A vaccination programme whose critics cite its visible side effects while the illnesses it prevented, which no one sees, go uncounted
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option D is Correct: Visible side effects are noticed while prevented illnesses are not, just as visible rent rises are noticed while the rises that did not occur are invisible. Each side has material for its case because one outcome is seen and the counterfactual is not.

• Why Option A is Wrong: This concerns selection and credit, not the invisibility of a counterfactual.

• Why Option B is Wrong: This concerns narrow preparation leading to success, with no hidden counterfactual.

• Why Option C is Wrong: This concerns a bet on a marketing strategy; nothing is seen versus unseen.

💡 Approach: Extract the structure: visible harm versus invisible avoided harm. Reject options that share only a topic (teams, exams, sales).

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: A) Concentrated local opposition to housing may prevail even where the wider gains from new building exceed the local costs.
B) Moving land-use authority to regional governments would solve the political and the knowledge problems at the same time.
C) Adding new market-rate housing always reduces rents in nearby buildings, so that rises observed after construction must be a mistake.
D) High-density districts are unhealthy in all circumstances because crowded places transmit disease more readily than other places do.
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option A is Correct: Paragraph 5 says costs are concentrated and visible, benefits diffuse and invisible, and concentrated losers are better organised, so local decisions predictably favour the losers.

• Why Option B is Wrong: The passage says moving authority upward solves the political problem 'at the price of a knowledge problem', so it does not solve both.

• Why Option C is Wrong: 'Always' is too strong: the evidence is described as mixed, and rent rises may be real but smaller than they would otherwise have been.

• Why Option D is Wrong: Paragraph 7 says dense districts with good transport and services can be productive and pleasant, so 'unhealthy in all circumstances' contradicts it.

💡 Approach: Inference questions reward the option that follows closely from a stated mechanism. Absolutes ('always', 'all circumstances', 'both at the same time') are warning signs.

title: Great Men, Structures, and the Discipline of Counterfactual History

passage:
Few questions in historical writing are as old, or as stubborn, as whether history is made by individuals or by forces. Thomas Carlyle held that the history of the world is the biography of great men. Tolstoy, in War and Peace, ridiculed the idea, arguing that Napoleon was carried by events rather than directing them, and that a leader who believes himself in command resembles a child holding the reins inside a carriage and imagining that he is driving it. Marxist and later structural historians sided with Tolstoy, and for much of the twentieth century the profession treated the great man as an embarrassment, a relic of the royal chronicle, in which the deeds of kings stood in for the experience of everyone else. In recent years, however, individuals have returned to serious scholarship, not as heroes but as variables: people whose presence or absence, it is argued, made a measurable difference, and whose influence can be estimated with the same statistical tools that are applied to economies and elections.

The question can be made sharper by asking what would have happened otherwise. Every claim that an individual mattered is a counterfactual claim: had Lenin not reached Petrograd in April 1917, or had a particular bullet missed a particular leader, events would have differed in some specified way. Historians have long distrusted counterfactuals as parlour games, but they cannot avoid them, since any statement of cause implies a comparison with a world in which the cause is absent. The real issue is not whether to reason counterfactually but how disciplined the reasoning is. A counterfactual is credible, on one influential account, when it requires changing very little, a minimal rewrite of the past, and when the world it describes is one that contemporaries thought possible. The more that must be altered to reach the imagined outcome, the less the exercise tells us.

Social scientists have tried to test the role of individuals with natural experiments. One strategy exploits chance: it examines leaders who died in accidents or from natural causes while in office, whose successors were therefore not selected for any trait connected to the country’s circumstances. A study of such cases found that the sudden replacement of a leader had measurable effects on economic growth in autocracies, but little in democracies, which suggests that individual discretion matters where institutions do not constrain it. The finding is elegant, but it carries limits. It measures the average effect of a leader across many cases, and so says little about any particular one; it covers a certain kind of event, accidental death, and a certain kind of outcome, growth rates; and it cannot distinguish a leader who changed a country from one who merely changed its statistics. Nor is it obvious that a result obtained for modern states can be carried back to earlier centuries, when the machinery of government was thinner and a ruler’s personal choices counted for more or, possibly, for less.

Defenders of structural explanation reply that leaders are themselves products of structures. A revolutionary movement needs revolutionaries; had Lenin not existed, the argument goes, someone similar would have emerged to fill the position, because the conditions that created a demand for such a figure would also have supplied one. This line has force where conditions are strongly determining, but it risks becoming unfalsifiable. If every individual’s absence is answered by the claim that a substitute would have appeared, no evidence could ever show that a person mattered; the argument has been protected from refutation by being made too general. Moreover, even if a substitute appeared, the substitute would not have been the same person, and the differences between them, in timing, temperament and decisions, may be exactly what shaped events. A replaceable position does not imply a replaceable person.

Another distinction helps. Individuals can matter in at least three ways: by determining which of several possible outcomes occurs, by changing the timing of an outcome that was coming anyway, or by shaping the manner in which the outcome is reached. Debate often proceeds as though only the first counts, so that a leader who merely hastened or delayed what would have happened is dismissed as unimportant. But timing and manner are not trivial. A war that ends a year earlier, or a reform achieved by negotiation rather than bloodshed, differs profoundly in human terms, even if the long-run destination is the same. A historian who ignores such differences in the name of structural inevitability confuses what is statistically predictable with what is humanly negligible.

A further difficulty is that the evidence is itself shaped by the beliefs under test. Memoirs, speeches and official histories are written by people with an interest in presenting their decisions as decisive or, when events went badly, as forced upon them by circumstance. Leaders claim credit for outcomes they merely witnessed and disown outcomes they caused. A historian who relies on such sources inherits their bias; one who discounts them discards the best evidence of what was considered and decided. There is no neutral position from which the documents can be read, and the choice between the great-man view and the structural view often precedes, rather than follows, the reading of the evidence.

What emerges is less a contest with a winner than a division of labour. Structures set the range of what is possible and make some outcomes far more likely than others; individuals operate within that range, and matter most where the range is wide: at moments of crisis, when institutions are weak or contested, and when a decision must be made once and cannot be reversed. This is a more modest thesis than either Carlyle’s or Tolstoy’s, and it has an unwelcome consequence for both camps. If individuals matter unevenly, then no general answer to the question is possible, and every claim about a person’s importance must be argued case by case, with the discipline that the counterfactual method demands and the humility that the evidence requires.

questions.question: Which of the following counterfactual claims would the author’s criteria in paragraph 2 rate as the most credible?
options: A) Had Napoleon been born a century earlier, Europe would have enjoyed an unbroken peace until the beginning of the twentieth century.
B) Had the bullet missed a leader by a few centimetres, he would have gone on to announce the policy that his advisers had drafted.
C) Had the Roman Empire adopted steam engines in the first century, industrial society would have arrived a thousand years before it did.
D) Had the whole population of a country spoken a single language, its government would never have faced separatist movements of any kind.
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option B is Correct: The author’s test is a minimal rewrite of the past leading to an outcome contemporaries thought possible. A near miss by a few centimetres is a tiny change, and announcing a drafted policy was a live possibility at the time.

• Why Option A is Wrong: Changing Napoleon’s birth by a century rewrites a great deal, and the further claim of unbroken peace requires more alterations still.

• Why Option C is Wrong: Steam engines in Rome require enormous changes in knowledge and materials, and contemporaries did not consider them possible.

• Why Option D is Wrong: A uniform language alters the whole structure of a society, and the claim ‘never … of any kind’ stretches the consequences far beyond the change.

💡 Approach: Translate the criteria into a checklist (how small is the change; was the outcome thinkable then) and score each option. The smaller and more local the change, the more credible the counterfactual.

questions.question: The author notes that the study of accidental leader deaths measures ‘the average effect of a leader across many cases’ in order to point out that it:
options: A) says little about whether any particular leader, such as Lenin, was decisive in the events associated with his name
B) proves that individual discretion has no effect on economic growth in democracies in which institutions are strong
C) is unreliable, since leaders who die in accidents cannot be considered to be typical of leaders in general
D) overlooks the evidence from autocracies, in which the sudden replacement of a leader is rarely accompanied by any visible change
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option A is Correct: The sentence says the average across cases 'says little about any particular one'. An average effect cannot tell us whether a given individual was decisive.

• Why Option B is Wrong: The study found little effect in democracies, but the author never says this proves anything; and this is not the point of the average-effect remark.

• Why Option C is Wrong: The author presents the chance of the death as the study’s strength (successors not selected for the country’s circumstances), not as a source of unreliability.

• Why Option D is Wrong: The study found measurable effects in autocracies, so the option reverses the finding.

💡 Approach: Purpose questions: the answer is the limitation the author states right after the phrase ('says little about any particular one').

questions.question: The author’s objection that the ‘substitute’ argument risks becoming unfalsifiable rests on the idea that:
options: A) conditions that create a demand for a leader cannot also supply one, since demand and supply are determined separately
B) revolutionary movements are always led by the person who is best suited to the circumstances of the time
C) historians are unable to determine whether a given leader was in fact replaced by someone with similar views
D) if every absence is met with a claim that a replacement would have appeared, no evidence could count against it
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option D is Correct: The author says that if every individual’s absence is answered by a substitute claim, no evidence could show that a person mattered, so the argument is protected from refutation.

• Why Option A is Wrong: The author does not discuss separate determination of demand and supply; the supply claim is the structuralists’, which the author criticises on other grounds.

• Why Option B is Wrong: The passage never says leaders are always the best suited; it says a substitute would not be the same person.

• Why Option C is Wrong: Whether a replacement shared views is not the issue; the issue is that the claim can absorb any outcome.

💡 Approach: Unfalsifiable means no evidence could count against a claim. Pick the option that states this property, not one that merely says the claim is doubtful.

questions.question: Which of the following is the clearest example of an individual mattering by shaping ‘the manner in which the outcome is reached’ (paragraph 5)?
options: A) A president who signs a trade agreement a year before it would have been signed by his successor in any case
B) A general whose decision to attack decides which of two rival states will dominate the region for a century
C) A premier whose government achieves an inevitable transfer of power by negotiation and not by civil war
D) A scientist whose discovery would have been made at the same time and in the same way by any of her colleagues
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option C is Correct: The outcome (transfer of power) was coming anyway; what the individual changed was how it was reached, by negotiation rather than violence. This is the author’s own example of a reform achieved without bloodshed.

• Why Option A is Wrong: This changes the timing of an outcome that was coming anyway, which is the second category.

• Why Option B is Wrong: This determines which outcome occurs, which is the first category.

• Why Option D is Wrong: The discovery is identical in time and manner whoever makes it, so the individual makes no difference in any of the three ways.

💡 Approach: Sort the options into the three categories (which outcome, when, how). Only one option keeps the outcome and timing fixed while changing the means.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author’s claim in paragraph 6 that the choice of view ‘often precedes’ the reading of the evidence?
options: A) Historians who were shown the same documents before they had formed any view usually converged on the same view, whatever their training.
B) Memoirs and official histories are often written long after the events they describe, and by people who had an interest in the outcome.
C) Historians trained in the structural tradition tend to give greater weight to economic documents than do historians trained in other traditions.
D) Leaders have in many cases claimed credit for outcomes that were in fact produced by their subordinates and advisers rather than by themselves.
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option A is Correct: If historians with no prior view converge on the same reading whatever their training, then the evidence, not a prior commitment, is driving the conclusion, which directly undercuts the claim.

• Why Option B is Wrong: This supports the author’s point about the bias of sources and says nothing about the order of view and reading.

• Why Option C is Wrong: Different weighting by tradition fits the claim that prior commitments shape how evidence is read, so it strengthens the claim.

• Why Option D is Wrong: This repeats the author’s point about leaders claiming credit and is consistent with it.

💡 Approach: Weaken by attacking the causal order the author asserts (view first, evidence second). The only option that shows evidence producing the view is the one that works.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author’s conclusion?
options: A) Structural forces determine history so completely that the role of any individual can be dismissed as a matter of timing alone
B) Great individuals are the true makers of history, and structural historians have ignored the evidence of the most important crises
C) The role of individuals in history cannot be studied at all, since all the evidence has been shaped by the beliefs under test
D) The importance of individuals varies with circumstances, so each claim about a person must be argued case by case
questions.explanation:
🧠 Detailed Option Analysis:

• Why Option D is Correct: Paragraph 7 says individuals matter most where the range of possibilities is wide, and that since they matter unevenly no general answer is possible; each claim must be argued case by case.

• Why Option A is Wrong: The author explicitly rejects dismissing timing and manner as negligible, and calls the structuralist position as immodest as Carlyle’s.

• Why Option B is Wrong: The author calls the thesis more modest than Carlyle’s and denies that structure can be ignored.

• Why Option C is Wrong: The author says the evidence is biased and not neutral, but still demands case-by-case argument with discipline; study is difficult, not impossible.

💡 Approach: Conclusion questions: the answer should include the author’s qualified middle position. Extremes in either direction are traps.

title: Patents, Exclusivity, and the Uneasy Economics of Invention
